newsitem.title: ITALY: Padania? The road map may take some time.
newsitem.headline: Padania? The road map may take some time.

text.p: Separatist leader Umberto Bossi intends to declare independence for the "federal republic of Padania" on Sunday after a three-day journey across northern Italy. But don't try to buy a road map just yet.
For cartographers, just as for most ordinary Italians, the exact geographical confines of the "republic" Bossi plans to proclaim in Venice remain vague.
"What is 'Padania?' Nobody has yet explained it properly because they don't know themselves," commentator Norberto Bobbio wrote in the Turin newspaper La Stampa on Saturday.
Bossi, whose journey to "independence" has produced reams of newsprint but little reaction from the prospective citizens of "Padania", disagreed.
"Padania exists," the fiery separatist declared repeatedly at rallies on Saturday along the river Po which cuts across northern Italy from the Alps to the sea.
"The people of Padania are Celto-Venetian," added Bossi, whose speeches regularly rail against "Latin" corruption and what he identifies as Mediterranean failings.
According to the "leghisti", the followers of Bossi's Northern League, the absence of Padania on the world's maps is all part of a historical plot, to be rectified fast.
"Padania exists, even if up to now it has paid the price of a deliberate policy of omission and oppression," declares a League pamphlet handed out to reporters at the weekend.
"No other great nation in the world has been subjected to such a violent and systematic attempt to cancel and suppress its identity as Padania," the leaflet added.
It described Padania, which takes its name from the fertile Po valley, as "a hitherto hidden region, a country that has not yet found adequate recognition".
On banners, T-shirts and souvenirs sold at Bossi's rallies, maps of Padania are to be found, however.
All depict it as the current boot-shaped Italian state, severed at the knee and without the toe and heel.

The League recently declared that Padania was all the geographical area of northern Italy, from Slovenia in the east to France in the west, as well as the central regions of Tuscany, Umbria and the Marche on the Adriatic.
Bossi has said Venice would be the capital.
The German-speaking Alto Adige, French-speaking Val d'Aosta and Slovene pocket around Trieste would be autonomous with special statutes within a federal "Padania".
However even that is not the whole story in Italy, a nation which has been united only since 1870 and which still contains a plethora of languages and ethnic groupings.
When Bossi came ashore at the small town of Boretto, south of Mantua, on Saturday after travelling by catamaran from Cremona he was greeted by a large banner.
"North Lazio: Rieti-Viterbo-Civitavecchia with the Northern League, with Padania" the banner declared.
None of the central -- some would say southern -- towns mentioned are within the geographical territory envisioned even by the League. Some bystanders were clearly bemused.
"It doesn't matter, Padania has no fixed borders," said Marcello Ricci, a Rome urinologist standing beside the banner. "Padania is a concept far more than a geographical region."
Ricci said that a cleansed Rome, the source of all evils to most League followers whose cars carry stickers proclaiming "away from Rome", could even form part of Padania.
"We hope to bring the borders of Padania down to the Garigliano," Ricci declared, referring to the border between Lazio and Campania, the region around Naples.
